name: MCL — superficial
description: The superficial MCL forms layer 2 of the medial knee: a flat band about 9.5 cm long from its femoral attachment just proximal and posterior to the medial epicondyle to two tibial attachments, a proximal one into soft tissue over the anterior arm of the semimembranosus just below the joint line, and a long distal bony one about 6 cm below the joint line, deep to the pes anserinus tendons. On MRI it is a thin, uniformly low-signal band on all sequences, separated from the deep MCL and meniscus by a thin fat plane, with no surrounding edema. Coronal PD/T2 fat-sat images show its whole length; axial images show its anteroposterior extent and its relation to the pes anserinus and semimembranosus.

normal_values.femoral_attachment_center: ≈3 mm proximal and ≈5 mm posterior to the medial epicondyle (cadaver); another series centers it 1–2 mm proximal, overlapping the epicondyle
normal_values.distal_tibial_attachment_below_joint_lin: ≈6 cm (mean 61–62 mm in two cadaver series; the linear footprint spans ≈4–7 cm)

variants_pitfalls: A thin stripe or small triangle of fluid-bright signal (up to about 4 mm) beside the MCL is common in normal knees: fat, the MCL bursa or a little joint fluid (Watanabe 1989). A sprain needs a valgus injury: grade 1 is high signal around a normal-looking ligament, grade 2 adds intrasubstance signal or partial fiber disruption, grade 3 is complete discontinuity.

Edema around the MCL without trauma is common in medial compartment osteoarthritis: 27 of 30 knees with medial OA versus 2 of 30 age-matched controls (Bergin 2002). Treat it as part of the arthritis, not a sprain, unless there was a valgus injury.

Distal tears are easy to miss: a wavy, redundant sMCL ('wave sign') suggests a tear at the tibial attachment. Check on coronal and axial images that the pes anserinus tendons still lie superficial to the sMCL; a distal stump flipped superficial to them (Stener-like lesion, 20 of 51 distal tears in Boutin 2020) blocks healing and is an indication to consider surgical repair.

Three fluid collections sit around the sMCL and are told apart by position: the pes anserine bursa lies between the pes tendons and the distal sMCL below the joint line; the semimembranosus–tibial collateral ligament bursa is an inverted U draped over the semimembranosus tendon, deep to the posterior sMCL (Rothstein 1996); the MCL bursa lies between the superficial and deep MCL at the joint line. A parameniscal cyst instead connects to a meniscal tear.

Ossification at the femoral attachment (Pellegrini–Stieda lesion) marks an old proximal MCL injury: on MRI an ossicle with marrow signal beside the medial femoral condyle and a thickened ligament, without the marrow edema of an acute avulsion.
In clinically 'isolated' ACL ruptures the sMCL was injured in 62%, mostly in its midsubstance (73%; femoral 23%, tibial 5%) (Willinger 2022), so check it on every ACL tear even without valgus laxity.
